title: Swap two column names
prompt: The new HR tool calls the employment type `status`, and today's `status` becomes `employment_status`. Write `solve(employees)` so it returns the employees table with those names.
rules: Rename `status` (active, on leave, terminated) to `employment_status`, and `employment_type` (full time, part time, contractor) to `status`. Both stay in their places.
Remove `termination_date`, which the new tool works out itself.
The result has exactly one column of each name. Keep every row and every value unchanged, missing values and duplicates included.
hints: Renaming `employment_type` to `status` while the old `status` is still there leaves the table with two columns called `status`.
Move the old `status` out of the way first, then give its name to `employment_type`.
`withColumnsRenamed` renames the dict's entries one after another, in the order you write them, so the order inside the dict matters too.
starter:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F


def solve(employees):
    # Rename status to employment_status and employment_type to status.
    return employees
explanation: The order of the renames is the whole question. `employees.withColumnRenamed("status", "employment_status").withColumnRenamed("employment_type", "status").drop("termination_date")` frees the name `status` before giving it away. The other way round, renaming `employment_type` first, leaves two columns called `status`, and the next rename renames both. Spark doesn't stop you: duplicate names are allowed until something refers to one of them. `withColumnsRenamed({"status": "employment_status", "employment_type": "status"})` works too, because it renames in the dict's order; with the entries swapped it fails the same way. Copying values with `withColumn` instead puts `employment_status` at the end rather than in its place.
